narration.full_text: The nervous system is crucial for control and coordination in our bodies, working alongside muscular tissues. It's essentially a sophisticated network made of specialized nerve cells, called neurons. These neurons are designed to conduct information very quickly through electrical impulses, transmitting messages from one part of the body to another. Think of it as your body's internal communication network. The nervous system is a system of conducting tissues that receives stimuli and transmits them throughout the body, forming a complex network of nerves. The basic units that make up this entire system are called nerve cells or neurons. When you experience something, like touching a hot object, special nerve cells called sensory neurons carry that information from the receptors to your brain. Conversely, motor neurons are responsible for transmitting information from the brain to your effector organs, which are mainly your muscles and glands, telling them how to react. A nerve impulse is the information itself, traveling through neurons in the form of chemical and electrical signals. These impulses are typically carried by the dendrites towards the cell body of the neuron. The neuromuscular junction is a critical point where a muscle fiber makes contact with a motor neuron. This is where nerve impulses, coming from the central nervous system, are transferred to the muscle. The impulses travel from the neuron to the muscle fibers using neurotransmitters, much like how impulses cross a synapse between two neurons. Actions can be broadly categorized into two types: voluntary and involuntary. Voluntary actions are those that require conscious thought and are performed knowingly. For example, speaking to a friend or writing a letter are actions you choose to do. In contrast, involuntary actions are not under your conscious control. They are automatic responses to a stimulus, happening without you actively deciding to perform them. A common example is unknowingly touching a hot plate and immediately pulling your hand away. This brings us to reflex actions. A reflex action is a quick, sudden, and immediate response of the body to a stimulus. Examples include the knee jerk reflex or the rapid withdrawal of your hand when you touch something hot. The pathway through which these nerve impulses travel during a reflex action is known as a reflex arc.
